#5371. Ripple's XRP Ledger Lending to Receive Repayment Fix

The XRP Ledger's lending protocol is in for a tidy-up of how loan repayments get rounded. In plain terms, the balance after each payment would match the schedule, the update has been discribed in the official Github pull request.

After an overpayment, TotalValueOutstanding is reset to the scheduled value of the new PeriodicPayment.

Under the LendingProtocolV1_2 amendment, each on-time LoanPay would bring TotalValueOutstanding down to the scheduled value with one payment fewer, capped at the rounded PeriodicPayment.

The first commit moves the scheduled-value calculation out of computeLoanProperties into a separate scheduledValue function, with no behavior change.

That way, LoanSet and LoanPay round it the same way. Zero-interest loans also need a floor on the principal part, because their value is rounded to nearest while the principal is rounded up. Tests run on Legacy, CashBasis and FixedPrecision vaults, with and without the amendment.

Today, each payment's value part is calculated on its own, so rounding can build up across payments. The last payment can then need one unit more than the rounded PeriodicPayment, and the value parts can alternate between payments.

With the change, a method called telescoping makes the value part of every on-time payment either the floor or the ceiling of PeriodicPayment, and at least one unit. The last payment becomes exactly the rounded PeriodicPayment.

There's little to no effect for users and investors today. The extra unit on the final payment changes little. Older loans that already carried one unit above their schedule simply keep it, so the last payment still needs the PeriodicPayment and a single unit, unless the borrower overpays first.

Small overpayments are mostly ignored; the transaction goes through successfully and charges no extra XRP whatsoever.

Activation date is yet to be determined: 80% of validators agreement is needed for two weeks in a row for the amendment to go through. No public vote for LendingProtocolV1_2 has been announced yet, so the timeline remains uncertain.

An anonymous Tornado Cash whale sent $7 million to Hyperliquid to open a large long on Bitcoin this morning. According to Lookonchain and Onchain Lens, the wallet went in with aggressive 20x leverage with the plan to profit from Bitcoin crushing Ether.

Large holders usually run funds through mixers to move capital privately or to get ready to cash out. This case is unusual as the movement of these funds had just previously been tracked to a chain of addresses belonging to the hackers who drained the derivatives platform Drift Protocol of $290 million in April 2026.

Some blockchain researchers warn against jumping to conclusions about where the funds came from. There's still no direct evidence: Tornado Cash covers its tracks well, and the link between the wallet and specific hacks rests only on circumstantial matches in volume.

After starting as a brand-new address that withdrew 3,100 ETH from Tornado Cash, the unknown later swapped all of the Ether through CoW Swap on the spot, locking in $6.92 million in USDC. From there, the money went to the decentralized exchange Hyperliquid as collateral for future trades.

On the exchange, the whale didn't try to guess where the market was headed and just split the collateral in half, turned on 20x cross leverage and built a position worth about $26 million in total. The position consisted of $12.84 million at an entry price of $75,762.2 and an Ethereum short of 5,740 ETH worth $12.83 million.

So far, the bet is working. Bitcoin is holding near local highs, and the gain on the BTC long fully covers the drawdown from altcoin short. Add to this the earnings on funding, collecting a regular premium from other traders for holding the ETH short.

This is a textbook dominance pair trade, where the investor couldn't care less whether the industry as a whole goes up or down and the only thing that matters is the spread - the price gap between the two largest coins.

If Bitcoin rises faster than Ether, or if Ether falls harder than Bitcoin in a broad market crash, the trade profits.

The math is elegant, but 20x leverage is always a high risk. Should Ethereum rip higher while Bitcoin stays stuck in a range, the margin will be wiped out in seconds as Hyperliquid's cross-margin system will force-close the orders, and the investor will lose the entire $6.92 million. The liquidation price is set at $37,014.09 for BTC and $3,343.60 for ETH.

#5369. How To Challenge A Monopoly In The AI Age

If you were in Silicon Valley in the late 1990s, today’s AI boom might feel familiar. In 1998 and 1999, internet traffic was roughly doubling every six to nine months. That was extraordinary growth in demand, and still, that pales in comparison to what we’re seeing unfold now.

Today, the four largest U.S. cloud companies are looking at more than $700 billion in capital spending this year, and the cumulative AI infrastructure spending is projected to reach $3 trillion to $4 trillion by 2030.

Nvidia arguably fired the starting gun in AI chips when Jensen Huang hand-delivered its DGX-1 to OpenAI in 2016. Today, it is a household name deeply embedded in the AI ecosystem, working with near-exclusive supply and investment deals.

With such a huge market under a seeming monopoly, where can competition — and the innovation that follows it — come from?

Part of the answer is that scale costs you speed, though when going up against an execution machine like Nvidia this is simply the baseline you have to solve for. The pace of change in AI outruns anything we saw in previous tech cycles: Model generations turn over in weeks, not years. The hardware beneath it has to keep shifting to serve them, and designing from first principles has real merit.

Hardware suppliers of the dot-com era followed the same peaks and troughs. Cisco, founded in 1984, dominated internet routing for most of the decade, and in March 2000 it was the highest market capitalization company in the world.

Then Juniper Networks, a startup where I was a founding engineer, shipped its first core router in 1998. Juniper went from a fairly anonymous upstart to 17% of the core router market at the end of 1999, then again to 38% in early 2001.

Challengers now can lean on history for some guidance.

First, don’t build a cheaper version of the incumbent’s product. Build a far better one. At Juniper, our bet was that the then-adolescent version of the internet was going to demand an exponentially higher throughput than before. Introducing an entirely new architectural approach to how routers are built, along with an innovative design philosophy focused on performance and reliability, we didn’t set out to sell a better router, so much as redefine what a core router had to be.

The boom in AI inference is today’s version of that strain on throughput. The initial hyperfixation on training AI models is fading, and the industry is collectively moving on to using them — known as inference. Inference is where AI’s promised productivity gains actually materialize, putting trained models to work across every task. As the enterprise applications for AI grow and become more complex, so too does demand for inference compute.

Google recently reported that it now processes more than 3.2 quadrillion tokens a month, up from 480 trillion a year earlier, as AI moves from chat to agents that plan and act on our behalf. Serving tokens at scale is a different beast from when it was just for model training, with different constraints on memory, power and cost.

The core principle we use applies to all sectors: Challengers have a better chance at optimizing for the market that will come, not the market that is already well-serviced by the incumbent.

Challengers start without the incumbent’s biggest asset: a reputation. Buying from the market leader is the safe choice, so a startup has to replace that trust with evidence. Every technological edge you can demonstrate and validate makes the next conversation easier, and over time that compounds into the credibility that an incumbent may take for granted.

To aid this, make migration as easy as possible. No one is wedded to a product out of loyalty. Inertia is one of the biggest strengths of an incumbent: the ease of continuing to do what has been done.

Unless there are clear economic and operational benefits, scale and performance advantages, more often than not, integrating new systems will not be worth the work involved in switching suppliers. Take any technical friction out of the equation, and you have a fighting chance with your improved product.

The internet transformed the world in ways that we couldn’t have predicted, and I have little doubt that the relentless pace and momentum of AI is resulting in changes that are quickly making our lives and work unrecognizable from the recent past. This is only going to accelerate. Monopolies in frontier technology look insurmountable right up until the work changes. What AI does is rapidly morphing and evolving.

There is comfort in that for founders, and in something else too: A small team can now achieve so much. Challenging Cisco in the late 90s and early 2000s meant building a nimble and dynamic organization, albeit much smaller — one that is far more capable, reactive and product-focused. Juniper numbered a few hundred people by the time it had significant market traction, compared to the thousands of employees at Cisco.

Our own company is now around 120 people, attempting what once took an army. That is what should keep the incumbents watching.

R K Anand is co-founder and chief product officer of Tensordyne, an AI inference company. He was a founding engineer and executive vice president of the data center business unit at Juniper Networks and began his career designing microprocessors at Sun Microsystems.

#5368. Bitcoin vs Gold: History Points to a Potential BTC Comeback in 2027

All reviews, research, news and assessments of any kind on The Tokenist are compiled using a strict editorial review process by our editorial team. Our company, Tokenist Media LLC, is community supported and may receive a small commission when you purchase products or services through links on our website. As of Tuesday, November 10, the Bitcoin vs gold race has an unusual score for 2026: both are losing. Bitcoin (BTC) is down 15.1% this year, and gold is down 5.9%.

That is rare. We compared the two assets’ returns up to November 10 in every year since 2015. Both were down at this point only twice before, in 2018 and 2022.

Gold is still ahead on the year. Gold futures trade at $4,086 an ounce, 23% below their record close of $5,318 on January 29. Bitcoin, at $74,259, is 40.5% below its record close of $124,753 from October 2025.

The calendar favors gold too. In each of the past 11 years, whichever asset led on November 10 also finished the year ahead.

But 2018 and 2022 ended the same way: Bitcoin hit its cycle low within six weeks and then beat gold by a wide margin the next year. So is 2026 setting up the same turn for 2027?

The two earlier cases point the same way, though two cases are a small sample to build on.

Both rebounds came in the year before a Bitcoin halving, the event every four years that cuts the number of new coins miners receive by half. The halvings fell in 2020 and 2024, and the next one is expected in 2028. That puts 2027 in the same slot as 2019 and 2023.

This year itself looks settled. Bitcoin beat gold in 8 of the 11 full years since 2015, and gold won only in 2018, 2022 and 2025. In every one of those 11 years, the asset that led on November 10 stayed ahead to December 31. Gold leads by about nine percentage points, so history hands it 2026, its second win in a row.

Crypto Expert Report: What Are the 10 Next Crypto to Explode in 2026?

Gold’s slide has been steep for a metal. It closed at a record $5,318 on January 29, fell as low as $3,899 on October 30, and now trades at $4,086.

Investors have not walked away. Gold exchange-traded funds (ETFs) hold physical gold and trade like stocks. Worldwide, they added $2.7 billion in October, their fourth straight month of inflows, the World Gold Council reported on November 5. Their holdings rose 19 tonnes to a record 4,275 tonnes. Over the first ten months of the year, the funds took in $41 billion, the third-strongest run on record. North American funds were the exception, with small outflows.

Bitcoin has done better since February. Measured in gold, one Bitcoin bought 21.1 ounces on January 5. By February 23, that had fallen to 12.4 ounces, the lowest since March 2023. It now buys 18.2 ounces.

The gap since that February low is wide. Bitcoin is up 14.9% since February 23, while gold is down 21.8%. Since June 30, Bitcoin has gained 26.8% and gold 1.2%.

Discover: Bitcoin Miner and Whale Signals Spike on Binance: CryptoQuant Lays Out a Three-Part Test for a New Rally, and BTC Has Passed One

Both assets face the same test today. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes October’s consumer price index (CPI), the main measure of inflation, at 8:30 a.m. in New York, or 13:30 UTC.

Bitcoin trades at $74,278 ahead of the release. On Sunday, it fell to $73,510, its lowest price since August 21.

On the daily chart, where each candle covers one day, Bitcoin sits below both of its exponential moving averages (EMAs), averages that give recent prices more weight. The 200-day EMA stands at $76,480 and the 50-day EMA at $79,124.

Crypto Expert Report: Follow The Money – Which Presales Are Attracting Crypto Whales in 2026?

For gold, the line to watch is $3,899, the October 30 low. In the Bitcoin vs gold race, gold is on track to take 2026. If Bitcoin holds $73,510 and its 2018 and 2022 pattern repeats, 2027 is the year history gives to Bitcoin.

Want to keep track of the largest startup funding deals in 2026 with our curated list of $100 million-plus venture deals to U.S.-based companies? Check out The Crunchbase Megadeals Board.

This is a weekly feature that runs down the week’s Top 10 announced funding rounds in the U.S. Check out last week’s biggest funding deal roundup here.

This week brought another plethora of large funding rounds for startups and growth-stage companies. Shield AI, a defense tech player focused on autonomy and virtual simulations, secured the largest financing, bringing in $2 billion. Next on the list was drone delivery provider Zipline International, which pulled in a fresh $1.5 billion.

Rounding out the ranks were good-sized financings for sectors including agentic AI, space tech and AI infrastructure.

1. Shield AI, $2B, defense tech: Shield AI, a developer of autonomy software and systems for the defense sector, along with simulation and synthetic reality technologies, secured $2 billion in equity funding and $500 million in debt financing. The equity included a $1 billion Series H led by Disruptive and Innovation X Capital along with a $1 billion structured equity investment from funds managed by Blackstone. The $500 million debt financing was led by JPMorganChase. San Diego-based Shield also said it is acquiring radar company Echodyne in a transaction valued at $5.3 billion.

2. Zipline International, $1.5B, drones: Drone delivery provider Zipline International raised $1.5 billion in late-stage funding at a $21.5 billion post-money valuation. Paradigm, WCM Investment Management and Layer Global led the financing for the South San Francisco, California-based company, which plans to use the money to expand its U.S. manufacturing facilities and increase hiring as it builds a nationwide drone delivery network.

3. CesiumAstro, $730M, space tech: Austin-based CesiumAstro, a developer of space and defense communications systems and satellites, closed on $730 million in Series D financing at a valuation of more than $4.5 billion. Janus Henderson led the equity round, and the company also secured $100 million in debt financing through the Export-Import Bank of the United States and JP Morgan.

4. Northwood Space, $375M, space tech: Torrance, California-based Northwood Space, a developer of ground infrastructure to support satellite systems, picked up $375 million in Series C funding. Andreessen Horowitz and DFJ Growth led the financing for the 3-year-old startup, which raised its Series B about nine months ago.

5. Applied Compute, $350M, AI models: Applied Compute, provider of a cloud computing platform that enterprises and developers use to train and run large AI models, announced $350 million in new funding at a $3.25 billion valuation. Elad Gil led the financing, joined by a long list of investors including Nvidia. The San Francisco-based company, which launched 18 months ago, said its annual recurring revenue has already topped $100 million.

6. Harbinger, $240M, electric trucks: Harbinger, a startup known for electric truck technology that has been expanding into battery storage and defense applications, secured $240 million in Series D funding. Tiger Global, Capricorn Investment Group and Ridgeline led the financing for the Garden Grove, California-based company.

7. Sentra, $150M, AI data security: Sentra, a provider of agentic data security tools, closed on $150 million in a strategic investment led by Capital One Ventures. Founded in 2021, Sentra has headquarters in New York and Tel Aviv.

8. Traversal, $120M, agentic AI: Traversal, a startup building AI agents for enterprise site reliability engineering, secured $120 million in new funding at a $1 billion valuation. Kleiner Perkins, Redpoint and Khosla Ventures co-led the round for the New York-based startup.

9. Ocient, $100M, agentic AI: Chicago-based Ocient, a provider of agentic AI for enterprise with a focus on data analytics, picked up $100 million in Series C funding co-led by BOKA Capital and OCA Ventures.

10. (tied) Tutor Intelligence, $75M, robotics: Watertown, Massachusetts-based Tutor Intelligence, a startup focused on robot foundation model training and building robot workers, raised $75 million in Series B funding led by Andreessen Horowitz.

10. (tied) Kalepa, $75M, insurtech: Kalepa, a provider of AI tools for the insurance industry, secured $75 million in Series B funding at a $470 million valuation. Updata Partners led the round for the New York-based startup.

We tracked the largest announced rounds in the Crunchbase database that were raised by U.S.-based companies for the period of Oct. 31-Nov. 6, 2026. Although most announced rounds are in the database, there may be a small time lag, as some rounds are reported late in the week.

#5365. ZetaChain's 55M ZETA Burn Isn't a One-Time Event: What Proposal 2 Really Does

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

ZetaChain's Governance Proposal 2 would halt its L1 around Dec 9, mint ZETA 1:1 on Solana and burn about 55M ZETA in monthly installments. Voting closes Nov 7.

Headlines are calling it a 55 million ZETA burn. Read the proposal's own schedule, though, and nothing close to 55 million disappears on the day the chain halts. The figure is real, but it arrives in twelve installments over 2027.

ZetaChain published Governance Proposal 2 on November 4, and its announcement post lays out the mechanics. About 55 million ZETA of undistributed validator emissions will be burned monthly through 2027, following the schedule on which they would have been emitted. The roadmap in the same post puts the pace at twelve monthly burns of roughly 4.6 million ZETA each, from January to December 2027.

That detail changes how the number should be read. Most of the early flash coverage collapsed it into a single burn, which implies an immediate supply shock. The staged schedule tells a different story. These tokens were never going to circulate, because they are validator rewards for an L1 that is about to stop. Burning them on the original emission timetable keeps the published release schedule intact and introduces no new mechanism, as ZetaChain's FAQ puts it.

Governance Proposal 2 builds on Proposal 68, which approved the move to Solana in September with 99.4% in favor. Proposal 2 supplies the mechanics. Voting runs 72 hours and closes on November 7, and ZetaChain says nothing moves unless it passes.

If it does pass, every ZETA balance is recorded at snapshot block 20,755,000, expected around December 9. The ZetaChain L1 halts at that same height and isn't restarted. Claims open the same day through the ZetaHub migration portal, and ZetaChain's new private AI app, ZetaLabs, launches alongside it.

The proposal also pairs the migration with a new whitepaper, which ZetaChain calls the document of record for the token after the move.

The snapshot goes well beyond a simple wallet count. It records liquid, staked, unbonding and unclaimed-reward balances. Staked ZETA is credited automatically, so nobody has to unstake, and exchange balances convert without any action from holders. Staking rewards stop at the snapshot height.

Holders who want to claim directly face a short process. They connect the wallet that held ZETA, sign a message naming a Solana wallet, and receive the full balance shortly afterward. The claim costs no fee and requires no SOL. According to the post, the portal asks only for a signature, never for a transaction or a seed phrase. A minimum of 10 ZETA at the snapshot is needed to claim.

Two edge cases deserve attention. First, ZETA wrapped or sitting in pools and contracts can't be claimed by a key, so holders need to unwrap and exit before the snapshot. Second, assets still held as ZRC-20 tokens at the snapshot can be claimed back on their original chain through a separate bridged-assets page, with a $5 minimum per token. Both are the kind of detail that catches people out when a deadline arrives.

On Solana, ZETA becomes a native SPL token under the same ticker, with 9 decimals and no freeze authority. The full snapshot total is minted before the portal opens, and then the mint authority is revoked, so no one can ever mint more. No third-party bridge is involved.

That sequence is the strongest holder protection in the plan, and it is also the part that can be checked in public. The supply stays capped at 2.1 billion less whatever has been burned, and ZetaChain says it will publish the SPL mint address and the migration program address before December 9. Once those exist, anyone can compare the minted total against the snapshot and confirm that the authority was actually revoked. That confirmation deserves the most scrutiny.

Meanwhile, the portal and its program are under independent review by Hacken, and ZetaChain says the portal opens only after the review is complete and the report is published. The ERC-20 version of ZETA on Ethereum is unaffected by the proposal. Purchaser and core contributor vesting completes on January 1, 2027, and ZetaChain says no newly released ZETA will be sold in 2027.

The biggest practical risk is inattention. Most holders don't need to do anything until December 9, but exchange users depend on each exchange's own conversion window, and anyone holding ZETA through a contract or pool has homework to do beforehand.

Scams add another layer of risk. Any migration with a claim portal invites imitators, and ZetaChain tells holders to trust only its official domains and social accounts. A simple rule of thumb helps here: a site that asks for a seed phrase should be closed immediately, since the legitimate flow only needs a message signature.

On the technical side, claims are checked against the published snapshot rather than the live chain, so they continue to work after the halt. ZetaChain says it will announce any change to the process in advance.

The vote decides the terms, not the direction. If Proposal 2 fails, the direction approved in Proposal 68 stands and ZetaChain returns with a revised proposal. Nothing moves on these terms.

If it passes, the sequence is clear. The security report, mint address and migration program address arrive before December 9. The snapshot, halt, mint and portal opening follow on the day, and the monthly burns run through 2027. ZetaLabs then adds a Premium tier in the first quarter of 2027, with ZETA as the token for access and payment.

Taken together, this looks more like a retirement plan for an L1 than a dramatic supply event. The burn is gradual, the mint is capped, and the claim process is simple on paper. Execution is what will matter most: the audit report, the published addresses and the clean revocation of mint authority. Those are the items to watch between now and December 9.

What lies behind the announcement is the conclusion of week-long retaliation with the HYPE community as holders of native Hyperliquid token needed to wait longer than others to be able to withdraw from Binance.

💁🏻‍♀️ Withdrawals have now been re-enabled for the following networks and assets: New: ✅ HYPE ✅ APT

The predecessor of this story is the biggest cyberattack in history when, according to the FBI and Chainalysis, the North Korean hacking group TraderTraitor emptied Binance's hot wallets for about $6.3 billion in a matter of 20 minutes. What happened next is the exchange blocking $3 billion with the help of Tether, Circle; its pledge to cover 100% of users' money from the SAFU fund; and thorough audits across Solana and Ethereum chains. Then, starting November 1, Binance started reopening tokens for withdrawal.

HYPE was the last to become eligible and the community behind DeFi giant met such a measure with discontent, crying about sabotage and unfair competition tactics. It's not that deep: Hyperliquid, being the headliner of decentralized finance, amasses a big share of the pie in on-chain derivatives trading, and of course this affects Binance's business.

The retaliation between the two has continued since 2025 when Hyperliquid founder Jeff Yan publicly accused Binance of lowering liquidations data after the October 10, 2025 event, when positions worth around $40 billion were marginally closed across the crypto market. Binance then delayed the spot listing of HYPE token until September 24, 2026 and gave it 'Seed Tag', which is usually applied to high-risk cryptocurrencies. Binance founder Changpeng Zhao diplomatically refused the accusations and said that strong decentralized exchanges on the contrary increase 'the pie' for the whole industry.

The delay indeed has a technical aspect. HYPE operates within its own Layer-1, HyperEVM. Auditing a custom blockchain architecture — not standard EVM or Solana-based — in the aftermath of such a hack requires more time and attention to be carried out properly.

In the wake of the cybersecurity crisis the pause was still interpreted as corporate vengeance. This makes Yi He's words and the demonstrative relaunch of withdrawals a sign that obligations for clients take priority over market rivalry.

NVIDIA tokenized stocks traded through a shock on Sunday, November 8, when news about Nvidia’s CEO broke while Wall Street was closed. At 20:12 UTC, CNBC reported that Nvidia’s board was investigating CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies suspect of spying for China.

The stock market was closed. Tokenized versions of Nvidia, which trade around the clock on crypto platforms, were not. Within 30 minutes, Nvidia’s market on Hyperliquid fell 3.3%.

By the time Wall Street opened on Monday, 18 hours later, the token traders had already found the price. Hyperliquid’s Nvidia market stood at $173.27 a minute before the opening bell. Nvidia opened at $173.07, just 0.1% away.

Nvidia reports earnings on November 17, after the market closes. So can tokenized stocks call the move again?

The weekend gave tokenized markets a clean test. Nvidia closed Friday at $186.64 on the Nasdaq, and nothing traded on Wall Street until pre-market trading opened at 4 a.m. in New York on Monday, or 09:00 UTC.

We tracked Nvidia’s price on Hyperliquid minute by minute. The market there is a perpetual contract run by trade.xyz, a type of futures contract with no expiry date that follows the share price.

Backed tokens moved the same way. NVIDIA xStock (NVDAx), a token on Solana backed by real Nvidia shares, fell from $188.13 on Sunday at 20:00 UTC to $175.98 by 08:00 UTC on Monday. Hourly prices on CoinGecko show the same overnight slide.

Crypto Expert Report: What is the Best Meme Coin to Buy and Forget Until the Next Bullrun?

The news pulled in traders. Between Friday’s close and Monday’s pre-market, $258.5 million worth of Nvidia traded on Hyperliquid.

That is 4.7 times the average of the four weekends before, when the same 60-hour window saw $33 million to $72 million.

The timing explains it. Over a normal weekend, almost nothing happens to Nvidia, so the tokenized market is quiet. This weekend, it was one of the few places where traders could act on the news for about 13 hours.

There is an irony here. On November 2, Nvidia joined the companies objecting to tokenized versions of their shares on OKXICE, the planned venue from NYSE owner Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) and the crypto exchange OKX.

Discover: JPMorgan and Coca-Cola Block Tokenized Stocks on OKXICE as Objectors Hit 33. Coinbase and Robinhood Stay Out of the List

The next big Nvidia news will also land when Wall Street is mostly closed. Nvidia reports its third-quarter results on Tuesday, November 17, after the market closes, with a call at 5 p.m. in New York.

The regular after-hours session runs until 8 p.m. in New York. From then until 4 a.m., tokenized markets are among the few places still trading Nvidia.

The test will be harder this time. Weekend news hit a quiet market with one clear direction. Earnings bring a flood of numbers at once, and the first move after a report often reverses.

Nvidia trades at $173.17 on the Nasdaq on Tuesday, down 3.1% after hotter-than-expected U.S. inflation data. It touched $170.12, its lowest price since March 31. It is 28% below its record close of $239.24 on October 6.

On Hyperliquid’s four-hour chart, where each candle covers four hours, Nvidia sits below both of its exponential moving averages (EMAs), averages that give recent prices more weight. The 50-period EMA stands at $189.53 and the 200-period EMA at $206.78.

For NVIDIA tokenized stocks, the weekend was proof that they can price news before Wall Street. On November 17, watch the tokenized price between 8 p.m. and 4 a.m. in New York for the first read on Nvidia’s earnings.

#5360. Paper Unicorns Are Cheap. Building A $1B Revenue AI Company Takes A Multimarket Cap Table

A $1 billion valuation still makes a startup a unicorn on paper. Yet when 250 companies joined The Crunchbase Unicorn Board in the first half of 2026, the speed of wealth creation raised another question: How many of these businesses can keep their customers once the initial excitement fades?

I would set a higher benchmark for unicorns with $1 billion in revenue sustained by customers who keep paying.

I spent five years at Harbin Institute of Technology and Shanghai Jiao Tong University, where “fail fast, improve faster” shaped my approach to building technology. Having studied in China before building an AI company in Abu Dhabi, I have also seen how the same growth story can raise different questions among investors, eventually boiling down to: “What will customers keep paying for?”

Fast revenue deserves attention. Founders who turn pilots into paying deployments are solving a real problem, and strong sales can make the next round easier. An annualized run rate built from discounts, experimental budgets or generous compute subsidies, however, offers little assurance that customers will stay.

Since 2023, the price of hitting a fixed level of AI performance has dropped thirteenfold every year. Startups that just resell model access now face brutal price competition. Look at OpenRouter and its $113 million Series B: developers can already swap between models through one shared interface.

Businesses built around proprietary workflows face a different test. Software embedded in a company’s approvals, records and daily decisions can be far harder to replace than the model doing the underlying work. I would check whether customers renew at full price and expand their contracts. Then I would see whether margins stay healthy after inference costs.

Once founders know who keeps buying, they should raise across regions, because a local backer can double as market entry. Borders barely slow an AI product down. Enterprise sales still depend on local budgets, procurement procedures and relationships. A foreign investor becomes valuable when those connections turn a product demonstration into a paid contract.

The $30 million Series A for London- and Gulf-based 1001 AI offers a useful example. U.S. venture firm Lux Capital led the financing, alongside Saudi PIF-backed Sanabil Investments. The deal cannot establish future retention by itself, but it shows how capital, talent and customers can sit on different maps, with engineers in London and customers in the Gulf.

Ask every investor what they bring besides money. One warm introduction to the right buyer can beat a higher valuation if it turns into a contract you can actually deliver and renew.

The choice between traditional venture funding and sovereign-backed money is often framed as a choice between fast and patient capital. I find the more practical distinction lies in the obligations attached to each check.

In conversations with U.S. and European venture investors, I have often been asked how quickly we could turn product adoption into repeatable sales before competitors caught up.

Venture firms need returns within their fund’s life. That puts commercial momentum and a sizable exit at the center of their investment decisions. The pressure can sharpen execution. It can also backfire when founders who chase fast expansion without counting delivery costs may fill their pipeline with discounted experiments instead of enduring enterprise relationships.

Sovereign-backed investors usually ask me a very different set of questions. They want to know where user data gets processed and which technical capabilities stay in the country. Will local customers still be able to rely on the service years from now?

Some funds carry an explicit domestic development mandate. For them, those concerns can count as investment criteria alongside financial returns. The upside is a partner who cares about local infrastructure and enterprise adoption. The price can be longer diligence and localization spending. Contract terms that make it harder to expand elsewhere can also cause a problem.

Neither mandate is universal. Many sovereign-backed funds pursue conventional financial returns, while traditional VCs can support long enterprise sales cycles. Government-affiliated capital doesn’t guarantee procurement wins, either.

Founders should read the fine print: governance rights, exclusivity requests, promised commercial introductions. Then judge whether the investor’s regional reach is worth the constraints.

The best capital strategy follows the customer’s path, from a working product to a renewal. Venture money speeds up development and sales once the business model works. Regional strategic investors earn their place when a new market’s infrastructure and procurement rules call for local expertise.

I would rather show an investor a small cohort of customers renewing without discounts than a glossy revenue forecast that depends on the next funding round. The numbers to watch are net revenue retention, production deployments and margins after delivery costs.

Market sentiment will keep minting and erasing paper unicorns every quarter. The founding teams that build $1 billion in lasting annual revenue will likely balance venture momentum with regional obligations. Their global cap tables will mirror the enterprise markets they serve.

Ilman Shazhaev is the founder and CEO of Dizzaract, an AI and gaming infrastructure company headquartered in Abu Dhabi and the largest game development studio in the Middle East. His work focuses on distributed AI infrastructure, human behavioral data and the interactive environments in which AI systems are trained and tested. Shazhaev is a United Nations expert under the UNODC program, advising on how AI can help solve social problems in developing economies. He is also the author of 46 scientific articles, including published research on AI that reads a player’s psychological state from ordinary gaming hardware, and holds 10 registered invention patents.

Dogecoin cofounder Billy Markus shared a lighthearted observation about Japan's unique dog culture in a post on X, pointing out the popularity of Shiba Inu dogs in Japan.

"Like, 50% of the dogs I see in Japan are Shiba Inu," wrote Markus, who goes by the online handle Shibetoshi Nakamoto.

like 50% of the dogs i see in japan are shiba inu i love japan

The Dogecoin cofounder's comment is based on his own observation when he was in Japan, where the Shiba Inu breed has deep cultural roots and is still one of the country's most recognizable native dog breeds. Markus' observation is noteworthy, as he is the cofounder of Dogecoin, a cryptocurrency that draws its origins from the Shiba Inu dog.

On December 6, 2013, Dogecoin was launched, taking influence from the famous Doge meme: an image of a very adorable Shiba Inu dog with multi-colored Comic Sans text that appears as the dog's "thought bubbles."

This famous meme was based on a 2010 photograph of a Japanese female Shiba Inu dog, Kabosu, adopted by Japanese kindergarten teacher Atsuko Satō from an animal shelter in 2008. This helped establish the dog-themed cryptocurrency trend that later inspired several other tokens, including Shiba Inu (SHIB).

Kabosu, a Japanese Shiba Inu, inspired a generation of online jokes and became the face of Dogecoin cryptocurrency. Kabosu was the face of the breezy Doge meme, her quizzical expression surrounded by an inner monologue of choppy phrases in bad grammar written in rainbow-colored Comic Sans font.

In 2010, two years after adopting Kabosu from a puppy mill where she would otherwise have been put down, Ms. Satō, a teacher from Sakura, east of Tokyo, took a picture of her pet crossing her paws on the sofa. She posted the image on her blog, from where it spread to online forum Reddit and became a meme that bounced from college bedrooms to office email chains.

This inspired Dogecoin, which was started as a joke by two software engineers, Billy Markus and Jackson Palmer, and is now the 12th largest cryptocurrency, with a market capitalization of $11.17 billion, according to CoinMarketCap data.

Kabosu, the dog behind the "doge" meme, died in May 2024 after 14 years of internet fame.

#5357. Series A In 2026: Capital Is Flowing Faster, But Fewer Startups Are Making The Cut

More money is pouring into Series A rounds, but it isn’t opening the door to more startups. U.S. companies have raised $42 billion at that stage this year through October, up roughly 60% year over year, while deal counts remain on pace with the past few years, Crunchbase data shows.

The numbers point to an increasingly divided early-stage market. AI is fueling demand for capital and helping some startups grow at unprecedented speeds, while others struggle to turn their first customers into repeatable sales.

Investors are responding by moving in opposite directions: Some are writing much larger checks at seed to get ahead of the competition, while others are waiting until Series B or beyond for clearer evidence that a business is taking off. (At Series B, too, we’re seeing a similar trend of fewer but larger deals.)

That leaves companies still proving their growth potential navigating a Series A funding crunch even as capital floods into the fastest-growing businesses.

The low point for Series A funding in the past five years was 2023, with $23 billion invested in U.S.-based startups. Series A investment totals each year since have grown, doubling this year compared to 2023.

At the same time, round counts have settled, averaging 1,200 companies funded at Series A at $1 million or more in 2023 through 2025. This year, the trend is holding, with round counts in that range, give or take 100 deals.

“On the application side, it’s a bit harder, and that’s where I think there’s more of a Series A crunch,” according to Siddharth Ramakrishnan, a partner at Scale Venture Partners, which primarily leads Series A and B rounds.

This dynamic — steady deal count despite much more money flowing — is also impacting how early-stage VCs invest.

Among investors, there’s more competition, especially at the early stage. In turn, VCs are increasingly pursuing one of two opposing strategies: either writing much larger checks much earlier, or holding back until later rounds, Ramakrishnan said.

With the first strategy, check sizes are getting much bigger, he noted, with $10 million to $20 million seed deals not uncommon. “Instead of waiting till the Series A, where they have $4 million in revenue and growing, you’re going to do it when they have $500,000 in revenue, they have a pilot, the team is smart,” he said.

Other investors are waiting to invest later. “ ‘I’m not getting any new information by the time they’re at $2 million in revenue from $500,000, so I’m just going to wait until they actually take off,’ and then you’re seeing a gap,” Ramakrishnan said, explaining the thinking behind this investment approach. “People are putting in a lot of money at the Series B, Series C onwards, because that’s when you get the signal that things are really working.”

Scale expects there to be a bit more variance in this current fund. Its preference is to stay at Series A and B risk profile, by “potentially pulling a little bit earlier and a little bit later and recreating it in the aggregate,” he said.

The firm’s most recent fund 8 is its largest to date at $900 million, up from its prior $600 million fund.

“We still think that Series A is a great place to be if you can make it happen, because it’s at that point where you ideally have enough information to make an informed bet, but not enough that there’s still some of the growth investors that are scared to come in,” Ramakrishnan said, “and so you get great companies at great prices.”

At each quartile, U.S. Series A rounds have trended up in size this year, Crunchbase data shows. So far in 2026, 10% of Series A rounds are $75 million and over, up from $50 million in 2025.

Those much-larger checks are translating into hypergrowth for some companies. “Instead of going zero to $7 million, which in the old world would have been amazing numbers, now there’s people going zero to $20 million, or zero to $30 million,” Ramakrishnan said.

For founders, securing those larger checks often hinges on turning a handful of early customers into a repeatable sales process. Many startups get stuck in that transition, even as investors compete to back those that break through.

“If you have the ambition to build a world-class company, then you also need to raise a big Series A to expand and go abroad, take on different types of markets,” according to European seed investor Anke Huiskes of NP-Hard Ventures, whom I interviewed on-stage at the HumanX Amsterdam conference on AI earlier this year.

“I think the whole messy phase is in this go-to-market phase where you don’t really know who your ideal customer profile is,” said Huiskes, who invests at the seed stage in product-focused founders.

She’s seen startups get stuck when they have a few customers but aren’t growing fast enough. “A lot of the companies hang out here,” she said.

But for the companies who build that repetitive sales cycle, VCs are eagerly reaching out, she said: “And then I get a text, ‘Can you please give me an intro?’ And all of a sudden, I have 10 term sheets. So it’s really black and white.”

#5356. Vitalik Buterin Declares Ethereum (ETH) a Store of Value, Not Fee-Burning Token

The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Ethereum's intrinsic economics is rebuilding itself in motion with tech bugs and the macroeconomic picture overlaying each other in the span of 48 hours. The week wraps up for a major alternative crypto project with a sudden Glamsterdam hard fork stop after testnet launch revealed a dangerous bug in the fee recalculating mechanism, brutally breaking the logic in smart contracts.

As the Ethereum community debated the ability of the network to sustain on old power, Vitalik Buterin showed up with a manifesto which completely zeroes out all the panic around mainnet's decreasing revenue. The "red line" behind Vitalik's updated vision is that the community should stop being fixated on the idea of ETH as "fee-burninng token". For a basic blockchain layer worth $270 billion, attempts to build evaluation on the amount of gas burned are a dead end. For Vitalik, the novel of "ETH as store of value (SoV)" is much more viable amid all the global uncertainty around.

This U-turn, taken by a key visionary of the ecosystem, happened at $2,240 for ETH and may drastically change all the plans developed with a focus on Glamsterdam architecture. The hard fork was initially projected for the logic of blockspace surplus, not the deficit. Ecosystem builders are already readying expansion of L1 capacity with the help of EIP-8037 (tariffs calibration) and EIP-7928 (parallel production) with an aim to raise gas limits up to 200 million units. The logic is that the excess of free space will cheapen the transactions, while token burning rates will gradually be cut.

The market saw a risk of deflation in this concept. Vitalik took a front-step. By his estimates, the historical peaks of burning through EIP-1559 "never were as strong as they seemed". They were dependent on inner cyclical activity of crypto speculations. And it itself was falling once every bear market started.

EIP-1559 is not going anywhere, and Vitalik openly says "don't be sad" if the volume of gas burned will forever stay below the 10% mark. The source of value for Ethereum lies in completely another dimension.

Solana's co-founder, Anatoly Yakovenko, unexpectedly aligned with Buterin on this matter. "You can't focus on fees as the products", he said, calling such an idea "absolutely meaningless". According to Yakovenko, the blockchain network must generate real value for the end users, not control the price of getting into the block.

Vitalik is absolutely right that you can’t focus on fees as the product. That’s absolutely meaningless. You need to pick a product, the thing that brings value to people, and do that really well.

There is lots of technical stuff and philosophy around, but what the missed deadline on the testnet and Vitalik's manifesto reveal is that Ethereum opts for long-term, secure, and even a bit boring stability of the basic layer. Infra doesn't try to flirt with the market through deflationary records.

#5355. Startup Founders Are Using AI To File Patents. Here’s Where DIY Becomes A Liability.

Patents can help startups establish competitive advantage, attract investors and protect innovations. But the traditional patent process is expensive, slow and difficult to navigate, particularly for companies with limited resources.

AI is changing that equation. General-purpose tools can research existing patents, document inventions and generate drafts that look like patent applications in minutes. Handling the process themselves can seem like an easy way for founders to save money.

But AI’s capabilities are jagged. AI can perform some tasks remarkably well while missing legal and strategic issues that determine a patent’s commercial value. An application can look sophisticated while providing little meaningful protection.

For example, a patent’s claims define its legal boundaries and what you can stop competitors from doing. Mistakes involving claim scope may remain hidden until an investor, acquirer or competitor scrutinizes the company’s intellectual property.

The question isn’t whether startups should use AI. It’s how much founders can safely do themselves and when legal expertise becomes essential.

Founders can use AI to organize technical documentation, summarize existing patents and identify potentially relevant prior art. Turning engineering notes into an organized invention disclosure, for example, can reduce preparation costs and help counsel focus on strategy.

But the opportunity extends beyond DIY. The right counsel can orchestrate AI across the workflow, coordinating invention discovery, drafting, drawings and quality checks. AI can help counsel explore alternative implementations with the inventors, identify disclosure gaps and check support for claims. Attorneys can direct that work, evaluate the results and connect each step to best protect business needs.

That combination can produce more comprehensive applications with substantially greater efficiency. It is fundamentally different from generating an application with a chatbot and asking a lawyer to review it afterward.

The cheapest filing option is not necessarily the most economical. A poorly prepared application can create false confidence while leaving valuable innovations exposed.

Counsel can help decide what to patent versus maintain as a trade secret, prioritize filings within the company’s budget and assess deadlines before disclosure or filing limits the available options. An internal process that competitors cannot observe or reverse engineer, for example, may be better kept as a trade secret.

Claim scope requires particular judgment. A fraud detection claim tied to one algorithm may leave competitors free to deliver the same functionality using another. Overly broad claims may overlap with existing technology. Valuable claims target what competitors must do to compete. Ideally, a single identifiable competitor can infringe them, and that infringement can be detected and proven.

The specification must describe alternatives and variations that support broader claims later without unnecessarily limiting their scope. AI can assist, but strategic judgment must guide the work.

Filing volume says little about commercial value. Investors and acquirers will look beyond the number of pending applications to ask:

AI’s greatest value is not simply generating more applications at lower costs. It is making meaningful protection more accessible without sacrificing legal judgment.

Founders should ask how a firm coordinates its AI tools and legal expertise, not simply whether it uses AI. The answer should explain how that process improves both efficiency and substance.

Ultimately, the most expensive patent mistake may be discovering too late that a DIY application never adequately protected the innovation on which the business was built.

Michael Drapkin is a founding partner of Landfall IP, an AI-native patent law firm based in Boulder, Colorado. He previously founded one of the largest electronics and computer patent prosecution practices in the U.S. at an Am Law 100 firm and was named U.S. Patent Practitioner of the Year by Managing IP in 2022.

Nathan Mutter is managing partner and founder of Landfall IP, an AI-Native law firm. He has served as top outside counsel at Oura, Coinbase, Rubrik, Salesforce 1 and many others. Mutter pioneered the creation of automation systems and tools that enhance efficiency across all aspects of legal services. His clients include both startups and large public companies.

#5354. Flare CEO Pushes Back Against XRP 'FUD'

Flare CEO Hugo Philion has expressed his frustration about recent fear, uncertainty, and doubt (FUD) around XRP and reiterated that the future of the cryptocurrency should not be centered solely around Ripple.

The Flare CEO recently addressed in an X post the constant habit of XRP holders to evaluate the future of the cryptocurrency through the prism of what Ripple is doing and what it isn't.

"The value and narrative of XRP should never have been viewed as being dependent on the actions of a single actor," the Flare CEO said.

The Flare CEO emphasized that XRP holders should instead concentrate their efforts on finding ways to improve the usability of the cryptocurrency.

In this context, Philion said that XRP holders need to consider three main questions.

The first question is what XRP holders are actually doing to utilize their XRP holdings. The second is how they can convince potential investors to hold XRP.

Finally, the third point that the Flare CEO mentioned is that the XRP community should find a way to transform XRP from a predominantly speculative asset into usable capital.

"And that's part of the reason we created Flare because we feel like there's always been more that can and should be done with XRP," the Flare CEO added.

Besides, the Flare CEO also invited XRP holders to try Flare. According to Philion, it's a way to make XRP less dependent on Ripple.

The Flare CEO's statements come amid increasing frustration around XRP and the lackluster performance of the cryptocurrency.

Over the past year, the price of XRP has gone down by around 50%, and at press time, the price of the cryptocurrency stands at $1.16.

Recently, Ripple's former chief technology officer David Schwartz also faced some criticism over the poor performance of XRP. Schwartz noted that his influence on the XRP price was very limited.

One X user raised a question about whether FLR holders are doing enough to demonstrate the value of the cryptocurrency, especially when it's possible for XRP holders to use Flare's decentralized finance ecosystem without purchasing FLR.

Still, Philion dismissed the claim that there is no need for FLR when using FXRP (a tokenized version of XRP on Flare).

"It's incorrect btw that you can use FXRP without needing FLR," the Flare CEO clarified.

According to Philion, what Flare Smart Accounts do is simply abstract away the need to manage FLR and make the experience more convenient. At the same time, FLR is used to pay transaction fees on the underlying networks.

Besides, the Flare CEO also underlined that in the long term, there should be more use cases for the token apart from transaction fees.

"Usage is important. Need to get fee generation going in a broader way in the ecosystem," he added.

#5353. webAI Releases TwIL-8B: A 5 GiB Open-Weight Reasoning Model With a 98.2 MATH-500 Score

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

webAI's open-weight TwIL-8B posts 98.2 on MATH-500 and says it tops Gemma 4 31B. The card's own footnotes show why the comparison deserves a re-run.

A model small enough to run from a roughly 5 GiB file on a CPU now claims a 98.2 on MATH-500. The most revealing line in its model card isn't a score, though. It's a footnote saying the competitor numbers were never re-run.

webAI released TwIL-8B as an open-weight model on November 4, and its Hugging Face model card leads with ambitious numbers. The 8.8B-parameter reasoning model is post-trained from IBM's Granite 4.2 8B using full-parameter supervised fine-tuning, followed by GRPO/DAPO reinforcement learning. A final length-aware RL stage produces the "balanced" variant, which is the default.

The card reports 98.2 on MATH-500 and 88.3 on AIME 2025. It says TwIL-8B posts the highest MATH-500 and LiveCodeBench scores in its comparison group, which includes Gemma 4 31B at about 3.5 times its size. That claim is worth testing, because small models that beat larger ones are exactly what open-weight users want to hear.

On MATH-500, the card lists TwIL-8B at 98.2, Qwen3.5-9B at 96.6 and Gemma 4 31B at 87.9. On AIME 2025, TwIL-8B scores 88.3 against 87.1 for Gemma 4 31B. On LiveCodeBench, TwIL-8B scores 81.6 against 80.0, though that figure carries a dagger marking it as measured on the verbose variant, not the default balanced one.

The card is also more candid than most. It says TwIL-8B is not a knowledge model. GPQA Diamond comes in at 70.2, trailing Gemma 4 31B by 14.1 points, and the model also trails on MMLU-Pro and HLE. There is no safety or preference tuning beyond what Granite carries, and the license is non-commercial. That honesty makes the claims easier to weigh.

Here is where the headline gets complicated. TwIL-8B's scores come from webAI's own internal high-effort pass@1 runs. The card states that competitor scores are published figures and were not re-run.

Gemma 4 31B's 87.9 on MATH-500 comes from Red Hat's evaluation of an FP8 build, using the lighteval harness, not from Google. The card itself notes that this figure is unusually low and may reflect answer extraction. In other words, the 10.3-point gap that anchors the headline compares one team's own harness against a third party's number that the card suspects may be understated.

None of this makes TwIL-8B's result wrong. It means the margin isn't established until both models run under the same harness, prompt and sampling settings. For reference, Google's Gemma 4 model card is the source for several of the other Gemma figures in the table.

Read the whole table and the picture is more balanced than the headline suggests. In the card's head-to-head summary, TwIL-8B beats Gemma 4 31B on 3 of 14 shared benchmarks and loses 11. It leads on MATH-500, LiveCodeBench and AIME 2025, but trails on AIME 2026 (88.3 against 89.2), HMMT Feb 2026 (68.2 against 77.2), GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro and IFEval.

The AIME 2025 lead is the shakiest. The card says AIME and HMMT sets have 30 to 33 problems, so one problem is worth about 3 points, and gaps of that size sit within noise. A 1.2-point margin is well under one problem, so the result is best read as a tie.

Against the closest same-size rival, Qwen3.5-9B, the card shows the models roughly level on contest math, with TwIL-8B using fewer tokens: about 19.5k per AIME 2026 problem against 31.2k. That efficiency claim may turn out to be the more durable one.

The card makes replication unusually practical. The Q4_K_M balanced GGUF weighs 4.98 GiB and runs through llama.cpp, with a command given in the card. Larger Q8_0 and F16 builds exist only for the verbose variant. The model also needs a big generation budget, since a short limit truncates its reasoning and scores far worse. The card suggests settings around 32,768 new tokens and a 40,960-token context.

Anyone planning a check should expect three catches. First, the card says all its scores were measured on bf16 weights, not the GGUF builds, so a CPU run tests a slightly different artifact, and the card expects small deviations, most likely at Q4_K_M. Second, MATH-500 is 500 problems and each answer can run to tens of thousands of tokens, so CPU testing will be slow. Third, the decoding setup matters, since the card says none of its numbers use low-effort or thinking-off modes.

For a fair comparison, the same prompt, answer extraction and sampling must be applied to Gemma 4 31B too, ideally at full precision.

The card also lists contamination caveats. Its training pools were decontaminated against AIME, HMMT Feb 2025 and 2026, MATH-500, GPQA, MMLU-Pro, HLE, IFEval, IFBench and LiveCodeBench using 13-gram matching. HMMT Nov 2025 and the HumanEval, MBPP and CRUXEval suites weren't in the decontamination set. The MATH-500 and AIME results fall inside the protected group, which counts in the model's favor.

Overall, TwIL-8B looks like a genuinely strong small model for contest math, code and instruction following, and the card is open about its weak spots. The claim to beat Gemma 4 31B is narrower than the headline suggests: a clear lead on one benchmark, a likely tie on another and a loss on most of the rest.

The useful next step is a same-harness run of both models, with the bf16 weights as a control for the GGUF build. Until independent results appear, the 98.2 is best quoted as webAI's reported figure, and the size-beating framing is better described as unproven than wrong.

#5350. The Crunchbase Unicorn Board Tops 1,900 Companies In October, With 34 Companies Joining — Half Under 4 Years Old

A total of 34 companies joined The Crunchbase Unicorn Board in October, adding more than $96 billion in value and $14.8 billion in total funding to the board. The board also reached a new record of 1,900 private companies last month, including an all-time high of more than 1,000 such startups based in the U.S.

Last month’s new unicorn cohort also highlighted how quickly this AI cycle is awarding some companies with billion-dollar-plus valuations: Half of October’s new unicorns are less than 4 years old, and nine companies that joined the board during the month did so via seed or Series A raises.

Leading industries for unicorn formation last month were frontier labs, agentic AI, aerospace and semiconductors. The U.S. accounts for 23 of the companies, while China and Korea each added three. Estonia added two, a record for the nation in a single month. Singapore, Germany and Japan each added one new unicorn.

Anthropic is seeking to secure up to $88.5 billion in its planned IPO and a concurrent private placement, potentially making it the largest-ever fundraise tied to a public market debut.

For the IPO portion of its fundraise, Anthropic plans to sell just over 800 million shares 1 at $70 to $78 each. At the high end, that would bring in around $62.5 billion — the largest ever IPO fundraise after SpaceX’s $75 billion offering.

Anthropic also expects to pull in another $26 billion from a private placement slated to close immediately following the IPO. Investors in this include AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron Technology, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC.

Put together, it’s a record-setting capital haul for a company making its market debut, which Anthropic is expected to do later this month on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT.

Anthropic also recently updated its financial disclosures, showing results through September of this year.

For the first nine months of the year, the company had $33.2 billion in revenue, up from $2.5 billion in the same period a year ago. It’s an astounding growth rate, albeit Anthropic is already known for this.

#5345. Base Switches Off Flashblocks as Denim Goes Live: The Migration Risks Behind 200ms Blocks

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Base's Denim upgrade replaced Flashblocks with five canonical blocks per second. What that means for sequencers, RPC providers and smart contract developers is where the real story sits.

For about sixteen months, Base's fastest blocks were only promises. Since November 5, they are the ledger itself.

Denim went live on Base mainnet on November 5, after activating on Sepolia on October 21.

According to the upgrade page, the chain now produces five complete canonical blocks every second instead of one every two seconds. Flashblocks, the preconfirmation layer that ran alongside the two-second blocks since July 2025, is retired.

Most coverage stopped at the speed figure. The sharper question is what separates a canonical block from a preconfirmation, because that gap decides what breaks and what improves for anyone building on the chain.

Those updates were the sequencer's early word on what the next block would contain. They were previews of pending state, and nothing in them had its own hash, state root or receipts until the two-second block was sealed. Developers therefore had to keep an early execution result mentally separate from a settled transaction.

Denim turns the 200ms unit into the real thing. Under Base's 200ms Native Blocks specification, every block carries its own number, hash, state root, receipts and forkchoice updates, and moves through the unsafe, safe and finalized stages like any other block.

The sequencer's job gets heavier and stricter. Instead of streaming fragments of a larger block, it has to build and execute a full block for every 200ms slot. The header keeps its timestamp in whole seconds, so Denim adds a metadata transaction, the BaseTime deposit, placed second in every block. It supplies the sub-second portion: 0, 200, 400, 600 or 800 milliseconds.

Timing rules are tight. Slots can't be skipped, and each block's full timestamp must land exactly 200ms after its parent's. That timestamp comes from a schedule tied to the Denim activation and the block number, not from the sequencer's clock, so wall-clock time only determines when a build begins. Once execution finishes, the client rejects any block that breaks the 200ms progression.

This removes a layer of ambiguity. A preconfirmation was only as strong as the sequencer's word, while a canonical block can be validated, replayed and challenged by any node running the same derivation rules.

App developers face the biggest practical shift. Flashblocks streams ended at activation, so anything built on newFlashblocks, pendingLogs or the pending block tag has to move to canonical subscriptions like newHeads and logs. The migration guide lists the API changes required.

The seconds-based timestamp field stays as it was for compatibility. Block, header, transaction, log and receipt responses now include optional millisecond fields, timestampMs and blockTimestampMs, derived from authenticated BaseTime data. They are left out when that data has been pruned or is unavailable. One tooling detail deserves attention: the spec warns that the plain Alloy AnyRpcHeader type drops unknown fields, so anyone who needs millisecond timestamps must use a different type.

Node providers will see heavier traffic too. Dwellir's analysis notes that any service doing work on every block now does it ten times as often. Five fetches a second replace one every two seconds. Denim improves latency without adding capacity, so infrastructure bills are likely to climb.

Finality hasn't gone away either. Faster production doesn't erase the confirmation policy an application picks, and each 200ms block still passes through the same unsafe, safe and finalized stages. Bridges and exchanges that wait for a specific stage before crediting funds may need to rethink how many blocks they wait for, since a block count no longer equals the same stretch of time.

This is the area that deserves the most urgent attention. Base's spec warns that block.number now advances ten times faster in real time, while block.timestamp still ticks in whole seconds. A contract that treats a block count as a duration will see that duration collapse to a tenth of what its authors intended.

The affected patterns are common ones. Timelocks and cooldowns measured in blocks expire in a tenth of the time. Vesting and emission schedules run ten times faster. Per-block rate limits reset five times a second instead of once every two seconds, which lifts the effective per-second limit tenfold. Governance voting windows set in blocks shrink the same way. Uniswap V3-style TWAP oracles stay accurate, but a fixed observation cardinality now covers less wall-clock history, so long lookbacks can revert sooner.

Contracts built on block.timestamp are unaffected. Where a block count can be adjusted through governance, teams plan to divide it by ten. Where it is hardcoded into an immutable contract, the spec says it can't be retuned after activation, which leaves migration as the only fix. Denim also tightens transfer rules for Base's B20 token standard, and transfers to a token's own address now revert.

The coming weeks will show how much of this stays theoretical. Three things are worth tracking: whether any immutable contract with block-count logic misbehaves, how providers cope with the jump in per-block requests, and whether apps built around Flashblocks have fully moved over.

Denim looks like a cleaner design than the layer it replaced. A preview mechanism gives way to a block anyone can verify, and developers pay for it with a real migration. Speed grabbed the headlines, but the lasting change is that Base's sub-second confirmations now stand on the same footing as the chain's ordinary blocks.

#5343. Exclusive: Nubank Alum Raises $14M For Colombia’s Palomma To Tackle Rent Payments, Landlord Financing

In 2020, Cipriano Echavarría was working at Morgan Stanley in New York and weighing his next career move when he noticed a plaque on his desk. Among the names of people who had sat there before him was David Vélez.

He looked up the name. Vélez was not only a fellow Colombian from his hometown of Medellín, but also the founder of Brazilian digital bank Nubank. Echavarría took a photo of the plaque and messaged him on LinkedIn, asking for career advice.

It turned out that Vélez had an opportunity for Echavarria: Nubank was about to announce its expansion into Colombia and hire a launch team. By late 2020, Echavarría had returned home to join it, with plans to eventually start a company of his own.

Now Echavarría’s Medellín-based startup, Palomma, has raised $10 million in Series A funding led by Mexican venture firm Cometa to expand its financial services business for landlords, tenants and property managers, Crunchbase News has exclusively learned.

The financing brings Palomma’s total funding to $14 million, including $4 million in previously undisclosed funding, according to Echavarría, its co-founder and CEO. Participants include Volpe Capital, Clocktower Technology Ventures, Tekton Ventures, Simma Capital and Yango Ventures, alongside existing investors Y Combinator, 17Sigma, Nido Ventures and Norte Ventures.

Palomma says its annual recurring revenue has grown thirtyfold in 18 months to about $3 million. It processes about $130 million in monthly rental payments, serving more than 200,000 tenants through over 500 property managers in Colombia. It estimates $1.5 billion in annualized rent payment volume.

The company will use the funding to expand in Colombia, develop additional AI and financial products, and prepare to enter other markets. It is considering Mexico, Brazil and the Spanish-speaking U.S. market, although Echavarría said Colombia remains the priority.

“We want to win Colombia,” he said in an interview.

Palomma’s business combines software that helps property managers handle leasing inquiries, customer service and collections with a payments system for collecting rent and paying landlords. Those relationships let it sell financing, rental guarantees, and other financial products to tenants and property owners.

After nearly two years at Nubank, Echavarría went on to found Palomma with Felipe Monsalve and Nicolás Gómez del Campo, MIT-trained engineers with experience at Meta, Cobre and JP Morgan. The founders entered Y Combinator in January 2023 intending to build an account-to-account payments processor for Spanish-speaking Latin America. Growth was largely flat during the first year, Echavarría said. But then property managers began asking for help collecting rent.

It soon became apparent that there were problems on both sides of the transaction. Tenants paid rent early in the month, but got their paychecks in twice-monthly installments. Meanwhile, landlords depended on rental income but struggled to borrow against it or protect themselves when tenants stopped paying. Property managers handled collections and payouts through labor-intensive processes, Echavarría said.

Rather than acquire tenants and landlords as customers individually, Palomma decided to reach them through the companies managing their properties.

The team decided, “let’s basically use the property managers as a distribution channel,” Echavarría recalled.

Property managers get access to Palomma’s AI software, which handles tasks such as leasing conversations. It then offers to process their rent payments. Those payments give the company a record of rental income and tenant payment histories that it can use to assess applicants for financial products.

From there, Palomma offers services for both tenants and landlords. Palomma Plus gives tenants rewards and credit-building benefits, while Palomma Advance lets landlords collect up to 12 months of future rental income upfront. Palomma Protect covers rental income if a tenant defaults. The company is also developing Palomma Flex, which would let tenants split their monthly rent into two installments.

Property managers pay a subscription fee for the AI software, and Palomma earns a percentage of rent through its payments and financial services.

Getting customers to adopt more of its services has helped drive Palomma’s growth. The company reports net revenue retention of 390% after 12 months, meaning revenue from an existing group of customers nearly quadrupled, even after accounting for customers who left or spent less.

Overall, the decision to combine AI leasing software, payments and financial services reflects Echavarría’s view of what it takes to build a large business in Latin America. He pointed to U.S. companies such as EliseAI, Bilt, TheGuarantors and Flex as comparisons for different parts of Palomma’s business.  Echavarría believes that reaching a similar scale in Latin America requires a wider range of products.

“In the U.S., you can build one solution and be really large because the market allows it,” he said. “In Latin America, if you want to be really large, you need to do all the things.”

AI also helps decide which tenants qualify for rental guarantees. Palomma’s leasing agent communicates through WhatsApp and collects application documents. The company claims that it can then deliver an approval in under 30 seconds. The company draws on information from leasing conversations and rental payment behavior to assess applicants.

The company’s rental guarantees put Palomma on the hook if tenants don’t pay. The startup initially takes on that risk itself, but Echavarría told Crunchbase News it was working to finalize a partnership with an insurer that would share the risk and let Palomma offer more guarantees.

The startup is also using AI to keep its team small. As of Nov. 4, it had 18 employees, up from about 14 when it closed its Series A roughly three weeks earlier. A single customer service employee works alongside AI agents to support the roughly 200,000 tenants paying rent through Palomma’s platform, Echavarría said.

The startup operates on the premise that AI can make real estate financial services cheaper to provide, much as mobile technology helped digital banks compete with lenders that maintained large branch networks. Longer term, Palomma also plans to expand beyond rentals into homeowners association payments and residential property transactions.

Pepe Bolaños, managing partner at Cometa, said Palomma stood out for its founding team and the opportunity to modernize Latin America’s fragmented rental market. In Colombia alone, nearly 8 million households rent their homes, he noted.

“We look for companies tackling markets where outdated processes create an opportunity to build a proprietary data asset that can be leveraged and monetized through AI,” he wrote via email.

Bolaños pointed to Echavarría’s experience helping scale Nubank, and Monsalve and del Campo’s technical and financial backgrounds. In roughly 18 months, Palomma grew to process around $130 million in monthly rental payments and serve more than 200,000 tenants with about 14 employees, he said.

“That kind of execution is unusual. It convinced us that this team has what it takes to build a much larger business,” he added.

Unlike competitors focused on individual services, Palomma combines rent collection, tenant screening and rental guarantees, gathering data throughout the process, Bolaños said. Directly processing payments gives it insight into tenant behavior that can improve underwriting, flag potential defaults and support new financial products, while AI helps automate operations.

“We believe the combination of distribution, proprietary payment data and AI gives Palomma a competitive advantage that can become stronger as the company grows,” he said.

Losing the trendline again right after reclaiming it is how the biggest cryptocurrency has always behaved. Previous cycles played out like this:

The current chart is running the same script. From the $123,524 peak in October 2025, the coin bled 51.8% into the June cycle bottom at $59,517. Thorn isn’t selling certainty. Two cycles is a thin sample, and bottoms only get confirmed in the rearview mirror. The margin for error is wide: in 2012, Bitcoin broke down again from 18% above the line, while in 2015 it held from just 8% above.
